**A2: Scalability concerns.**
For convenience and ease of discussion, we have copy-pasted the experimental results of §5.1.2 most relevant to scalability concerns here, numbered as Tables 3, 4 and 5 in our author reply.

_Inner subroutine_: The inner LP subroutine of the grid search does depend on the number of groups, but 
only requires solving a modestly sized LP;
as discussed in Remark A.2., each iteration of the outer grid search solves an LP with
$\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}} |S_a| + |\mathcal{K}\_{\text{L}}|$ decision variables, 
and 
$|\mathcal{A}|+1$ linear constraints 
(for the simplex and post-processing per group), 
$2|\mathcal{A}||\mathcal{K}\_{\text{L}}|$ linear constraints (for the linear centroid bands), 
and $2|\mathcal{A}||\mathcal{K}\_{\text{LF}}|$ linear constraints 
(for the LF bands). 
Here, $|S_a|$ is the number of points in the support of the convex hull of the ROC curve for group $a\in\mathcal{A}$ and is typically small
both theoretically (Groeneboom et al., 2021), 
and empirically in our experiments, where it usually ranges between values such as 20 to 30. 
Moreover, 
 $|\mathcal{K}\_{\text{LF}}|$ and $|\mathcal{K}\_{\text{L}}|$ are the number of linear-fractional (up to 2 in our experiments) 
 and linear group fairness constraints (up to 3 in our experiments), respectively.
 
 Thus, for instance, if we have five protected attributes (like in the largest example that we consider), the total number of decision variables is roughly 100-150, and the total number of constraints is roughly 20. 
 This leads to modest-sized linear programs that current computational infrastructure can easily handle. 

_Outer search:_ The outer grid search over the centroids of the linear-fractional constraints does not depend on the number of groups $|\mathcal{A}|$, 
since we represent all linear-fractional and linear $\binom{|\mathcal{A}|}{2}$ pairwise disparity constraints as $|\mathcal{A}|$ linear disparity constraints via centroid-based linearization (see, e.g., §4.2). 

From a worst-case perspective, 
the outer grid search 
can depend 
exponentially in the number of linear-fractional constraints;
 however, this is not a practical limitation. 
 Indeed, first of all, the number of linear fractional constraints is always small, at most two, in our experiments. 
 Moreover, 
in practice we found  that using a relatively coarse grid of $25, 50$ or $100$ points works well when controlling for two linear-fractional constraints.
 This means that we need to search over at most 10,000 grid points, 
 which
 is very feasible and 
 takes a total of at most  4-5 minutes in our experiments and computational infrastructure. 
As suggested by comment B3 of Reviewer v8n8, and which is presently relevant here, we have added a new section with a 
sensitivity analysis for the granularity of the grid search in §A.6.3,
 where we show that in our experiments, even a smaller grid size of 50 or 25 can work quite well, and which does further reduces the total number of required grid point evaluations to up to 1250. 

_Running times_: Though our methods exhibit considerably larger running times for the setting of multiple linear-fractional constraints and multiple protected attributes (Table 5) 
we would like to note that this is due in part to the adaptive nature of our feasibility guard --
for this experiment, the guard is triggered approximately $p=2/3$ of the time (Table 4, in blue), which results in a bisection search on top of the outer-grid search.

The benefit is that our procedure finds a fair classifier with a minimal relaxation of the user-specified disparity tolerances, when the nominal disparity levels are ill-specified. 

When the feasibility guard is not activated, we see that the outer grid search is modestly timed, coming in at around 4-6 minutes per seed (Tables 4 and 5).

_Summary:_ Ultimately, our methods are able to scale in performance and speed to 
large datasets
such as ACSIncome
(which have hundreds of thousands of data points and
almost a dozen features)
for the challenging setting of controlling multiple linear-fractional and linear group fairness constraints (Table 3) -- a setting on which existing post-processing methods (see, e.g., Celis et al., 2019; Hsu et al., 2022) have been unable to demonstrate similarly strong empirical performance.

(for the LF bands). 
Here, $|S_a|$ is the number of points in the support of the convex hull of the ROC curve for group $a\in\mathcal{A}$ and is typically small
both theoretically (Groeneboom et al., 2021), 
and empirically in our experiments, where it usually ranges between values such as 20 to 30. 
Moreover, 
 $|\mathcal{K}\_{\text{LF}}|$ and $|\mathcal{K}\_{\text{L}}|$ are the number of linear-fractional (up to 2 in our experiments)

since we represent all linear-fractional and linear $\binom{|\mathcal{A}|}{2}$ pairwise disparity constraints as $|\mathcal{A}|$ linear disparity constraints via centroid-based linearization (see, e.g., §4.2). 

_Intersectional fairness._ We note that our method is not immune to the curse of dimensionality when considering intersectional subgroups —- however, this phenomenon is an inherent challenge in the broader intersectional fairness literature (Kleinberg, 2018; Gohar & Cheng, 2023).

Nonetheless, techniques developed for the intersectional setting can be readily incorporated into our pipeline; e.g.,
aggregating / smoothing estimates across related subgroups or  employing adaptive constraint selection to prioritize the most informative intersections.
These strategies have been used in prior work to mitigate small-sample issues in intersectional analysis, and they apply directly to our framework because our post-processing approach operates entirely on estimated group-conditional operating characteristics. We view extending ROC-F with these intersectional tools as an important direction for future work.

Any algorithm for working with small data sets is potentially susceptible to the sampling error inherent due to a small sample size. 
Prior methods
for fair classification are not an exception, and they are often 
significantly 
affected by limited dataset sizes: 
under standard datasets and similar split ratios for training, post-processing, and evaluation, our empirical analyses in §5 illustrate 
that 
existing post-processing methods like Celis et al., 2019; Hsu et al., 2022

In contrast, 
our method demonstrates strong empirical performance on relatively small, standard datasets like COMPAS with $\approx$5000 samples.
This demonstrates that our method is relatively stable to small dataset sizes, especially when compared to prior methods.

summary.value:
This paper introduces a method for jointly optimizing multiple fairness constraints under approximation thresholds. The method leverages the ROC to satisfy linear fractional fairness constraints, and provides extensive analytical results on the framework.

The authors empirically evaluate on standard fairness datasets, and demonstrate near-oracle performance over multiple fairness measures, with a principled and flexible delta-approximate fairness.

strengths.value:
1. The model is well-motivated and the authors situate their work well in the introduction. The application of the ROC is intuitive to a novice reader at a conceptual level.

I would like to thank the authors for a very thorough and well-structured rebuttal. The additional material—particularly the new Lawschool dataset, the grid-sensitivity analysis, the relocation of technical definitions, and the clarification of denominator guards and the Oracle baseline—substantially improves the clarity and self-containment of the submission. The added theorem in §4.2 and the expanded methodological explanations in the appendix also help contextualize some of the earlier claims. That being said, after carefully reviewing the responses, several aspects of my original evaluation remain only partially addressed:

1. Dataset breadth and empirical scope.
Although adding Lawschool strengthens the empirical section, the three datasets used (COMPAS, ACSIncome, Lawschool) remain quite similar in structure: medium-dimensional tabular prediction tasks from U.S. socio-economic domains. The method’s ability to scale (and more importantly, to generalize) to substantially different domains still must be inferred rather than demonstrated. This limits the strength of any general empirical claim.

2. Baselines and positioning relative to in-processing methods.
I appreciate the argument that post-processing baselines already dominate or approximate reduction-based in-processing methods, especially for linear constraints. Still, the reasoning remains indirect. Since a central contribution of ROCF is handling heterogeneous combinations of fairness metrics, it would be informative to show at least an ablation where in-processing methods are run on the subset of constraints they can handle, so the reader can see concrete trade-offs in constraint families, accuracy, and interventions. As it stands, the empirical comparison remains narrower than ideal for a paper with broad claims.

3. Multi-class extension.
The new multi-class discussion in §A.3.5 is conceptually appealing and suggests natural generalization via confusion-rate polytopes. However, this extension is fully theoretical: no experiments, no complexity analysis, and no discussion of how the explosion in the number of vertices or the dimensionality of the rate polytope impacts the runtime of the outer search or the LP. Without empirical verification, the claim that the framework “naturally extends” to multi-class remains preliminary.

4. Theoretical additions.
The new theorem in §4.2 provides reassuring finite-sample bounds conditional on the score function. However, in real deployments, the base score function is rarely calibrated or near-optimal. My original concern (how error in the upstream predictor propagates into fairness feasibility and operating-point estimation) remains open. I appreciate that the authors acknowledge the technical difficulty of such guarantees, but the current theory does not substantially change the conceptual positioning of the work.

5. Practical considerations of the outer search and feasibility guard.
The sensitivity analysis is helpful and shows that extremely sparse grids perform poorly while moderate grids (25–50) work well. However, runtime in the multi-attribute, multi-LF setting remains high (several thousand seconds per seed in Table 5). For a post-processing method (whose primary promise is low deployment cost) this overhead is substantial. The feasibility guard is well motivated, but the uniform-relaxation design still limits expressiveness in settings where users may want to prioritize certain constraints.

6. Intervention optimality.
The authors clarify that AntiDiagonal and LabelFlipping are conditionally minimal interventions given the empirical ROC point, but not globally minimal. This clarification is appreciated. Nevertheless, one practical question from my review remains open: in which empirical regimes does each mechanism dominate the other? 

Overall, the authors have clearly improved the paper and clarified many technical points. The rebuttal increases my confidence in the correctness and engineering quality of the approach. However, the revisions do not fundamentally change the scope or generality of the work. My main concerns (dataset diversity, limited empirical baselines, the preliminary nature of the multi-class extension, and the practical cost of the outer search) remain only partially resolved. I therefore maintain my original overall assessment. The paper is strong in motivation, clarity, and methodological elegance, but I will keep my score unchanged.

**A4: Post-processing limitations.**
Post-processing 
approaches start with a fixed classifier and update it to aim at ensuring various forms of algorithmic fairness. 
This paradigm is one of the 
most popular and successful approaches towards reducing disparity because of a number of reasons including:
- Its lightweight nature (it does not require retraining a classifier from scratch)
- Broad compatibility (it can work with any pre-trained classifier).
For this reason,
post-processing algorithms have found successful application in a variety of domains (see e.g., Nandy et al., 2022; Weerts et al., 2023; Mackin et al., 2025, etc.)
and are particularly useful when access to the training data or re-training the base model is infeasible (see discussion in §A.1 of our work).

 Nonetheless, 
 as the reviewer points out, 
they come with the potential limitation that they do not update the learned representations of the underlying model. 
When this property is required, it is necessary to use alternative training paradigms, such as preprocessing or in-processing methods, for achieving algorithmic fairness. 
In future work, it will be an important question to study how our approach could be adapted to these alternative training strategies. 
For now, 
we would like to argue that
the post-processing paradigm is both practically useful and popular, 
and that our methods demonstrate significant improvement compared to prior state-of-the-art approaches in this area. 

**A5: Generalization beyond binary tasks.**
In the revised manuscript, we now provide an extension of our framework (namely, a description of the algorithms) for the multi-class case, 
following the formalizations of multi-class group fairness constraints in Alghamdi et al., 2022; Xian et al., 2024. 

At a high level, we show that our method naturally extends to settings with $C>2$ classes by replacing the ROC curve with a polytope of confusion-rate matrices, 
whose vertices correspond to deterministic multi-class post-processors. 
We describe how to construct this empirical polytope, 
how to impose multi-class analogues of demographic parity, equalized odds, and sufficiency constraints, 
and how to recover a realizable randomized classifier via structured mechanisms (e.g., label-flipping or anti-diagonal mixing).

This extension requires no new assumptions; it relies only on convexity and the same polytope-based optimization as in the binary case. Full details are provided in §A.3.5. of the updated manuscript.
This analysis suggests that our approach is indeed not fundamentally tied to the binary classification setting, but that similar ideas may extend to the setting of a multi-class classification problem.

We thank all of the reviewers for their insightful questions and comments. In the revised manuscript, we have made the following changes: 

- **New theoretical result.** A new theorem with finite-sample guarantees for the optimal fairness-constrained operating characteristic rates, conditional on a fixed score function; please see Theorem 4.2 in §4.2 of the revised manuscript.

- **New empirical analyses.** Added new empirical analyses with an additional dataset and a sensitivity analysis of the granularity of the outer grid-search; please see §5 and §A.6.3.

In our responses below, we have done our best to address all of the reviewers' points and would be happy to continue the discussion if there are any further or remaining questions.

**D2: Binary-only setting.**
Our assumption that the scores are continuous is not strictly necessary for our proposed procedure in the binary classification setting,
as the resulting convex hull of the ROC curve will be the same.
We have made this clarification by revising Footnote 8 in §A.2.1.

Comment A5 of Reviewer YVAP posed a similar question about the possibility of extending our method to the multi-class setting,
but we give a complete response here for convenience. 

In the revised manuscript, we now provide an extension of our framework (namely, a description of the algorithms) for the multi-class case, 
following the formalizations of multi-class group fairness constraints in Alghamdi et al., 2022; Xian and Zhao, 2024.

whose vertices correspond to deterministic multi-class post-processors. 
We describe how to construct this empirical polytope, 
how to impose multi-class analogues of demographic parity, equalized odds, and sufficiency constraints, 
and how to recover a realizable randomized classifier via structured mechanisms (e.g., label-flipping or anti-diagonal mixing).

This extension requires no new assumptions; it relies only on convexity and the same polytope-based optimization as in the binary case. Full details are provided in §A.3.5. of the updated manuscript.
This analysis suggests that our approach is indeed not fundamentally tied to the binary classification setting, but that similar ideas may extend to the setting of a multi-class classification problem. 

**D3: Baselines.**

We agree that in-processing approaches (e.g., Agarwal et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Prost et al., 2019)
provide an important point of comparison in the broader algorithmic fairness field.

However, 
among post-processing methods that do handle linear constraints, 
Xian and Zhao (2024) provide an extensive empirical study demonstrating that their post-processing framework performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods (in particular, those of Agarwal et al., 2018 and Zhang et al., 2018).
Since our baselines already include this method of Xian and Zhao (2024), our evaluation implicitly covers the performance range of those in-processing approaches.

More generally speaking, such state-of-the-art in-processing methods do not support sufficiency-based constraints (i.e., the common linear-fractional group fairness constraints of predictive parity and false omission rate parity), 
making a larger, direct comparison misaligned with the constraint classes studied in this work.

We have added this clarification in the amended introduction of §5. 

**D4: Feasibility guard uniformity.**
The feasibility guard, in full generality, doesn't strictly require a uniform relaxation of the fairness tolerances.
For ease of exposition, we chose this uniform expansion since it allows a simple bisection search on the (uniform) expansion factor. 
One can certainly develop more sophisticated search procedures that prioritize certain fairness constraints, 
but these are application-specific and outside of the scope of this work (see, also, discussion of feasibility guard in §A.2.1)

**D5: Intervention optimality.**
Our constructions choose intervention parameters that are optimal conditional on the empirical ROC curve: for a given target operating point, the intervention objectives 
of equation 24 and 25 (in the revised manuscript) 
compute the minimal mixing or flipping probabilities needed to achieve that point. 
In this sense, both _AntiDiagonal_ and _LabelFlipping_ minimize the population-level expected number of interventions for that particular functional form.

More generally, we do not claim that these mechanisms are ``globally optimal" 
among all post-processing rules for minimizing the intervention rate (cf. Def. A.3).
Establishing such optimality is challenging, even between our two mechanisms _AntiDiagonal_ and _LabelFlipping_,
because the minimal achievable intervention rate depends on the geometry of the empirical ROC curve and the baseline post-processor. 
Nonetheless,
it is still possible to prove finite-sample guarantees of our approach -- the manuscript will be further updated with such a new theoretical result soon (see also, above, the global comment to all reviewers).

In light of this, 
we view our intervention methods
as interpretable, analytically tractable, and, most importantly,
practically effective instantiations of the broader design space 
of all post-processing rules. 

We have added this discussion to §A.3.3 in our revised manuscript for clarification.

Clarity: Clearly written and well-modularized. Rate-space figures and Algorithm listings support understanding.

Significance: Offers a practical, easily implementable method to jointly achieve fairness notions that were previously handled separately. Useful for any group dealing with fairness auditing or deployment.

weaknesses.value:
Limited scope and datasets: Evaluation restricted to two small tabular datasets (COMPAS, ACSIncome). 

Binary-only setting: The framework and proofs assume binary classification with continuous scores; no discussion of multi-class, where scores live in the probabilistic simplex. The assumption that scores are continuous (“ties broken deterministically”) could fail in applications.

Baselines: Comparisons are mostly to post-processing methods (Hardt et al. 2016, Hsu et al. 2022); in-processing reduction approaches (Agarwal et al. 2018) could be included for a broader view.

Feasibility guard uniformity: The relaxation of fairness constraints is uniform; no discussion of prioritizing one constraint (e.g., EO) over another (e.g., PP). This limits interpretability of fairness–utility trade-offs.

Intervention optimality: The AntiDiagonal and LabelFlipping constructions are heuristically minimal but not formally proven globally optimal; empirical stability to hull noise could be further demonstrated.

questions.value:
Centroid grid sensitivity: How fine must the centroid grid be to approximate the true feasible region? Any quantitative link between grid resolution and sub-optimality?

Denominator constraints: How are $\epsilon_k$ parameters for denominator stability selected, and do they materially alter fairness feasibility for small groups?

Constraint prioritization: Could the feasibility guard relax only selected constraints (e.g., PP but not EO)? A weighted relaxation could make the framework more flexible.

Calibration drift: How robust is ROCF if the base model’s score calibration shifts between training and deployment?

Multi-attribute scalability: How does ROCF scale when there are many protected attributes or intersecting subgroups?

Dataset expansion: Adding a credit-risk or medical dataset would make results more convincing and highlight ROCF’s linear-fractional handling.

AntiDiagonal vs. LabelFlipping: Under what conditions does one yield strictly fewer interventions? An ablation or theorem would clarify.

Oracle definition: Clarify what makes the Oracle baseline “infeasible in practice” (e.g., requiring group labels at test time).

summary.value:
This paper proposes post-processing algorithms for achieving (multiple) group fairness (criteria simultaneously), covering criteria that can be expressed in linear or linear-fractional forms: this covers SP, EO, TPR/FPR parity, and predictive rate parity.  The focus is on binary classification and the attribute-aware setting (sensitive attribute can be used explicitly as input to the classifier/post-processor).

Given the ROC (i.e., feasible TPR-FPR tradeoffs) of the Bayes optimal score function:

1. With a reformulation trick, the authors show that, if the "centroid" of the group statistics of the fair classifier is known, then the fairness criteria can be expressed as linear constraints in terms of the group-conditional TPR and FPR.
2. If the performance of the classifier is a function of the TPR and FPR (e.g., accuracy), then the optimal fair classifier is fully characterized by its TPR-FPR tradeoff.

With these two facts,

1. The authors proposed a bi-level optimization procedure where the outer layer sweeps over the possible centroids, and the inner layer solves the fair classification with the linear constraints as a linear program. Finally, it returns the one with the centroids that leads to the best performance.
2. To return a classifier achieving a specific TPR-FPR tradeoff, two methods are proposed: one is based on randomly interpolating a thresholded classifier (which lies on the boundary of the ROC) and a input-independent randomized classifier (which lies on the diagonal), and another which is based on combining thresholding and label flipping.

strengths.value:
- To the reviewer's knowledge, this is the first paper proposing a post-processing based method for achieving fair classification on linear (SP, EO, TPR/FPR) and linear-fractional (predictive rate equality) fairness constraints simultaneously.
- Experiment results show good empirical performance.
- The reviewer finds the reformulation trick for "linearizing" the linear-fractional constraints interesting, and could be also be applied to the more general attribute-blind and multi-class setting (for representing the optimal fair classifier).

weaknesses.value:
- The fact that a bi-level optimization procedure involving a grid search for finding the optimal "centroid" is required is a bit dissatisfying, and suggests that the proposed algorithm may be hard to scale to more general settings.
- The lack of a sample complexity analysis (probably about the same as fitting a linear model with $O(K)$ parameters), and an error propagation analysis: if the upstream score function is non-Bayes-optimal, how much would it hurt performance and fairness?

**C1: Scalability concerns.**

Comment A2 from Reviewer YVAP raised similar concerns about the scalability of our method, and we copy and paste our response here for completeness and convenience.

For convenience and ease of discussion, we have copy-pasted the experimental results of §5.1.2 most relevant to scalability concerns here, numbered as Tables 3, 4 and 5 in our author reply.

_Inner subroutine_: The inner LP subroutine of the grid search does depend on the number of groups, but 
only requires solving a modestly sized LP;
as discussed in Remark A.2., each iteration of the outer grid search solves an LP with
$\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}} |S_a| + |\mathcal{K}\_{\text{L}}|$ decision variables, 
and 
$|\mathcal{A}|+1$ linear constraints 
(for the simplex and post-processing per group), 
$2|\mathcal{A}||\mathcal{K}\_{\text{L}}|$ linear constraints (for the linear centroid bands), 
and $2|\mathcal{A}||\mathcal{K}\_{\text{LF}}|$ linear constraints 
(for the LF bands). 
Here, $|S_a|$ is the number of points in the support of the convex hull of the ROC curve for group $a\in\mathcal{A}$ and is typically small
both theoretically (Groeneboom et al., 2021), 
and empirically in our experiments, where it usually ranges between values such as 20 to 30. 
Moreover, 
 $|\mathcal{K}\_{\text{LF}}|$ and $|\mathcal{K}\_{\text{L}}|$ are the number of linear-fractional (up to 2 in our experiments) 
 and linear group fairness constraints (up to 3 in our experiments), respectively.
 
 Thus, for instance, if we have five protected attributes (like in the largest example that we consider), the total number of decision variables is roughly 100-150, and the total number of constraints is roughly 20. 
 This leads to modest-sized linear programs that current computational infrastructure can easily handle. 

_Outer search:_ The outer grid search over the centroids of the linear-fractional constraints does not depend on the number of groups $|\mathcal{A}|$, 
since we represent all linear-fractional and linear $\binom{|\mathcal{A}|}{2}$ pairwise disparity constraints as $|\mathcal{A}|$ linear disparity constraints via centroid-based linearization (see, e.g., §4.2). 

From a worst-case perspective, 
the outer grid search 
can depend 
exponentially in the number of linear-fractional constraints;
 however, this is not a practical limitation. 
 Indeed, first of all, the number of linear fractional constraints is always small, at most two, in our experiments. 
 Moreover, 
in practice we found  that using a relatively coarse grid of $25, 50$ or $100$ points works well when controlling for two linear-fractional constraints.
 This means that we need to search over at most 10,000 grid points, 
 which
 is very feasible and 
 takes a total of at most  4-5 minutes in our experiments and computational infrastructure. 
As suggested by comment B3 of Reviewer v8n8, and which is presently relevant here, we have added a new section with a 
sensitivity analysis for the granularity of the grid search in §A.6.3,
 where we show that in our experiments, even a smaller grid size of 50 or 25 can work quite well, and which does further reduces the total number of required grid point evaluations to up to 1250. 

_Running times_: Though our methods exhibit considerably larger running times for the setting of multiple linear-fractional constraints and multiple protected attributes (Table 5) 
we would like to note that this is due in part to the adaptive nature of our feasibility guard --
for this experiment, the guard is triggered approximately $p=2/3$ of the time (Table 4, in blue), which results in a bisection search on top of the outer-grid search.

The benefit is that our procedure finds a fair classifier with a minimal relaxation of the user-specified disparity tolerances, when the nominal disparity levels are ill-specified. 

When the feasibility guard is not activated, we see that the outer grid search is modestly timed, coming in at around 4-6 minutes per seed (Tables 4 and 5).

_Summary:_ Ultimately, our methods are able to scale in performance and speed to 
large datasets
such as ACSIncome
(which have hundreds of thousands of data points and
almost a dozen features)
for the challenging setting of controlling multiple linear-fractional and linear group fairness constraints (Table 3) -- a setting on which existing post-processing methods (see, e.g., Celis et al., 2019; Hsu et al., 2022) have been unable to demonstrate similarly strong empirical performance.

**3. Multi-class extension (ctd.).** _Computational complexity_ In the multi-class setting, each group-wise confusion–rate matrix lies in an
affine space of intrinsic dimension $d = C(C{-}1)$, 
so the inner problem remains a polynomial-size LP in the
convex weights and fairness centroids, and the outer search over
$\vec q^{\mathrm{Suff}}\in\prod_{\hat c}\Delta^{C-1}$ has the same structure as
in the binary case. 

The principal open question is whether the empirical 
hull, 
constructed from pruning many deterministic classifiers over $\mathcal{D}_{\text{post}}$, 
remains small in practice, as it does in the
binary setting (e.g., $\approx 20$--$30$ support points per group even for datasets
with over one million samples like ACSIncome; see also §A.5). 

A direct analogue of the theory available in the
binary class setting (e.g., Grenander-style arguments for the
ROC frontier as in Groeneboom, 2021) is not yet available for multi-class confusion-rate matrices. We view developing a full theoretical and/or empirical characterization of the number of support points of this empirical hull as an
interesting direction for future work, 
but note that it 
does not affect the polynomial-time
solvability of each inner-optimization subproblem for any fixed number of classes.

Ultimately, we agree that the multi-class extension is primarily conceptual in the current work and, due to time constraints, leave concrete empirical results to future work and have made this clear in the revised manuscript. We respectfully note that our finite-sample guarantees do not assume that the upstream score function is calibrated or near-optimal.

our results explicitly quantify how any level of upstream error propagates into feasibility and operating-point estimation, which we believe answers the  reviewer's original concerns about whether "empirical stability to hull noise could be further demonstrated" and quantifying "[Calibration drift:] how robust is ROCF if the base model’s score calibration shifts between training and deployment?". Moreover, our bounds align with the conceptual claim that if the original score function is a poor predictor, then one should not expect any post-processing method to easily achieve fairness constraints (see, e.g., Kleinberg et al., 2016). 

With this added clarification (see the revised discussion preceding Theorem 4.2 in §4.2),

	We would like to argue that these overhead costs of our post-processing method are reasonable relative to pre- and in-processing methods that require access to the data used to train a model and/or re-training a model entirely, which may be computationally prohibitive (on the order of days/weeks even on state-of-the-art industry-grade HPC infrastructure) 
or altogether infeasible in practice (see, e.g.,  Dettmers et al., 2023, Groves et al., 2024, and our discussion in §A.1).

Thank you for this suggestion. We have added a new theoretical result, Theorem 4.2 in §4.2, 
which establishes sample-complexity guarantees for both risk generalization and fairness attainment of our procedure’s operating-characteristic solution, conditional on a _fixed_ score function --
in the special case where this score function is Bayes-optimal, the theorem yields a parametric $\tilde O(1/\sqrt{n})$ convergence rate, 
showing that our method can attain statistically optimal performance and fairness in the idealized limit.

For convenience, we reproduce the theorem statement below; the complete proof appears in §A.4.2 of the revised manuscript.

**Theorem:**
    Let $s:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{A}\to[0,1]$ be a fixed probabilistic predictor 
    and let $\mathcal{D}\_{\textnormal{post}}$ be an i.i.d. post-processing sample with
    group and group–label specific sample sizes $n_a$ and $n_{a,y}$, respectively, 
    with $n_{\min} := \min\_{a,y} n\_{a,y}$ for $a\in\mathcal{A}$ and $y\in\{0,1\}$. 
    Also, let
    $\widehat\varrho = \\{\widehat{\vec \rho_a}\\}\_{a\in\mathcal{A}}$ be the lifted operating characteristics returned by our empirical region search procedure
    (i.e., Algorithm 2 in §A.2.1) with grid steps $h_k$ for each linear-fractional centroid and with
    $\varepsilon_k$ as the denominator guards.
For $\delta>0$, define for $j \in \{0,1\}$,
\begin{equation}
        \eta_{a,j}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2n_{a,j}}\log\frac{4m}{\delta}} + C\cdot 
        \sqrt{\frac{1}{2n_{a}}\log\frac{4mK}{\delta}},
\end{equation}
where $C>0$ is a universal constant that depends only on $\{u\_{k,a},v\_{k,a}\}\_{a\in\mathcal{A}, k\in\mathcal{K}}$, 
but not on $n_{a,j},m,K$, or $\delta$. 

Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$,

$\Big|J(\widehat\varrho)-J(\varrho^\star)\Big|
    \lesssim
    \sum\_{a\in\mathcal A}\big(\eta_{a,1}+\eta_{a,0}\big)
    + \sum\_{k\in K_{\mathrm{LF}}} h_k
    + \max\_{k\in K_{\mathrm{LF}}}\varepsilon_k,$

and for every fairness metric $k\in K\_{\mathrm{LF}}\cup K\_{\mathrm L}$,

$ \max\_{a,a'}
    \big|
    G\_{k,a}(\widehat\rho_a)-G\_{k,a'}(\widehat\rho_{a'})
    \big|
    \lesssim
    \delta_k +
    \max_{a}(\eta_{a,1}+\eta_{a,0}).$

Developing error propagation bounds with the Bayes-optimal regression function 
is non-trivial for our approach,
since we work directly on the empirical ROC curve: 
establishing such results would require characterizing this ROC curve's behavior both along its trajectory as we sweep the threshold $t$ in $1(s(x,a)>t)$ and within the model space (e.g., $s(x,a)$ are 3-layer hidden neural networks). 
This control of the ROC curve geometry is interesting, though it would seem to require novel proof ideas and tools not standard to common empirical process theory, so we leave these results to future work.

More generally speaking, 
sample complexity and error propagation results exist in the broader algorithmic fairness literature (see e.g., Kleinberg, 2018; Celis et al., 2019; Xian & Zhao, 2024)

However, we would like to argue that such results are ultimately unable to
bridge the gap between theory and practice, as such methods exhibit subpar empirical results unlike our approach (see empirical analyses in §5). 
With this newly added theoretical result, our approach is both empirically and theoretically well motivated, and
we leave it to future work to develop similarly rigorous results for error propagation bounds.

summary.value:
This paper presents ROCF (Fair Classification via Operating Characteristic Feasibility Regions), a post-processing framework for achieving approximate group fairness under multiple constraints such as demographic parity (DP), equalized odds (EO), and predictive parity (PP).
Instead of retraining models, the method intervenes directly on the operating characteristics (TPR/FPR) of a pre-trained classifier. It identifies feasible fairness-adjusted points using each group’s convex hull and post-processes predictions to reach those points. The approach extends to multiple protected attributes and supports linear-fractional fairness metrics.
Experiments on COMPAS and ACSIncome show that ROCF achieves approximate fairness across several criteria with minimal accuracy loss and few label interventions, outperforming prior post-processing baselines (Celis et al., 2019; Hsu et al., 2022).

strengths.value:
Novel geometric perspective: Optimizing fairness directly in ROC space via convex hulls is elegant and intuitive.
Handles multiple fairness criteria: Supports several linear and fractional constraints simultaneously, a limitation of most existing post-processing methods.
Practical deployment path: Works on top of pre-trained models, making it applicable when retraining is infeasible.

weaknesses.value:
Limited dataset diversity: Evaluation on only two benchmark datasets limits generalization; larger and more complex domains should be tested.
Scalability concerns: The grid search may be expensive when handling many groups or fairness constraints.
Sensitivity to data size: Since ROCF relies on convex hull estimation, small or noisy samples may affect feasibility, but this is not quantified.
Post-processing limitations: As with all post-processing methods, bias in the learned representation remains unaddressed.

questions.value:
Complexity and scalability: How does the computational cost of the grid search scale with the number of fairness constraints and protected groups?
Generalization beyond binary tasks: Could the ROC-based formulation extend to multi-class or regression settings, or is it inherently tied to binary classification?

We would also like to argue that basing experimental results around such datasets in the socio-economic domain is considered standard in algorithmic fairness literature -- e.g., COMPAS (Larson \& Angwin, 2016) and AdultCensus (Kohavi, 1996) (from which ACSIncome is based on) have been used as benchmark datasets in this subfield since its inception. 

More broadly speaking, these standards are intended less for immediate practical deployment and more so for establishing the method’s effectiveness. To these ends, we have demonstrated that our approach, ROCF-AD/LF, works and favorably scales across a wide range of sample sizes, as reflected in our experiments on the -- now 4 -- COMPAS (\~5k samples), BiasBios (\~25k samples), Lawschool (\~100k samples), and ACSIncome (\~1.6 million samples) datasets.
